Payer-Provider Data Infrastructure

Sagebrush Health

Sagebrush runs 12 rheumatology, infusion, neurology, and infectious-disease clinics across three states — which means Todd Lefkowitz's team is negotiating and operating against a different Medicaid MCO and commercial payer mix in Nevada, Connecticut, and South Carolina, while high-cost biologic infusions (Humira, Remicade, Orencia, Rituxan) generate constant prior-authorization and eligibility traffic that has to clear before a chair is ever scheduled.

Why now: Sagebrush is a boutique, HRSA-grant-backed network still adding clinics across three states, each with its own Medicaid MCO landscape and commercial payer contracts. Its clinical mix — biologic infusions, 340B-eligible sites, HIV/PrEP services with federal grant reporting — means eligibility checks, prior authorizations, and claims documentation are constant and high-stakes: a denied or delayed PA on a Rituxan or Remicade infusion is a rescheduled patient and idle chair time, and 340B participation raises its own documentation and audit burden. As the network grows into new markets, the payer-provider data plumbing that once worked for a single-state practice has to scale without adding headcount to chase eligibility and authorization status by phone and fax.

The Integration Pitch

Where managed care data actually lives at Sagebrush

Every new clinic Sagebrush opens is also a new set of payer contracts, a new Medicaid MCO panel, and a new pile of prior-authorization queues layered on top of Clinika and FollowMyHealth. For a Chief Managed Care Officer, that means the real workload isn't the EHR — it's everything that has to move correctly between the EHR and the dozens of payer portals, clearinghouses, and 340B systems that determine whether an infusion gets scheduled, billed, and paid.

That's the gap Vorro closes: not another portal to check, but a single integration layer that pulls eligibility, prior-authorization status, and claims data out of fragmented payer connections and pushes it back into the workflow your infusion coordinators and billing staff already use — so a Humira or Orencia authorization shows up before the patient does, not after they've been rescheduled twice.

On top of that data layer, Vorro's ambient documentation tools capture the clinical encounter itself — visit notes, ICD-10/CPT coding support, plain-language patient summaries — so the prior-auth packet and the claim are built from structured data instead of re-keyed after the fact. As Sagebrush adds sites in new states, that infrastructure scales with the network instead of requiring a new manual process for every new payer relationship.
